newsitem.title: USA: Fed proposes firewalls for U.S. bank subsidiaries.
newsitem.headline: Fed proposes firewalls for U.S. bank subsidiaries.

text.p: The Federal Reserve on Thursday proposed restricting capital transfers and loans between banks and bank subsidiaries engaged in non-bank activities.

Under the proposal, based on section 23A and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act, a bank could not invest more than 20 percent of its capital in subsidiaries and no more than 10 percent in a single subsidiary. Loans and similiar transactions would have to be conducted at "arm's length."
Similiar firewalls already apply to transactions between a bank and affiliates owned by the same holding company.
The proposal would not apply to bank subsidiaries that Congress has specifically exempted from section 23A in the past.
The rules are designed to safeguard the bank, and its federally insured deposits, from financial problems that occur in a subsidiary.

"The proposal would limit the bank's exposure to activities that Congress has determined to be too risky for the bank to conduct directly, and limit the transfer of the federal subsidy to such activities," the Fed said in a memo accompanying the proposal.

A legislative proposal to overhaul U.S. banking laws would impose similiar requirements on bank subsidiaries. Approved by the House Banking Committee last month, the bill is now before the Commerce Committee.
The Fed proposal marks a reversal from moves by the central bank over the past year to relax firewalls.
Some of the earlier proposals were strongly criticized by lawmakers as possibly increasing risks to the safety and soundness of the banking system.
In March, Senate banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato called one such proposal a "mad dash into an area that I think can jeopardize the taxpayers."
The central bank said it would accept comments on the proposal until September 3.
